content.text: When we first learned about the Binomial, we derived it using the
many coin flips example
. To derive the Multinomial Distribution, we can extend that metaphor to consider the probability of different outcomes of rolling many
dice

In this example we are going to imagine that we have a dice that can only have three outcomes. When you roll it you could get an A, a B or a C. What an odd dice! In order to make this metaphore as general as possible I am going to let our dice be even stranger! Imagine the probability of each of the three outcomes is not equally likely. Instead let
be the probability of rolling an A, and so on. To make things concrete image:
First here is a simulator where you can try rolling this dice 10 times:
Dice Roll Simulator
Exactly 4As 1B and 5Cs
Imagine you roll 10 dice, where each dice has three sides {A, B, C}. Here are all the orderings of outcomes for the 10 rolls where you get exactly 4 As, 1 B and 5 Cs:
Let's call each of these rows an "ordering" since each row is a unique way to order the 4 As, 1 B and 5 Cs. Let
be the number of unique orderings.
Exactly how many unique orderings are there of 10 letters with 4 As, 1 B and 5 Cs? We can solve this problem using
Permutations of Indistinct Objects
Each of these orderings can be thought of as one event, or outcome, of rolling 10 dice. Let's name
to be the event that we get the exact outcome in the
th row.
Let's calculate the probability of
. Eg:
(A, A, A, C, A, C, C, C, C, B)
In order to calculate the probability of this row, we need to know the probability of A, B, and C on our dice. Recall that:
The the probability of getting exactly the result in row 17 is going to be:
In fact that is the probability of every single row! Now we are ready to calculate the probability of exactly 4 As, 1 B and 5 Cs:

attrs.rawTex:
\begin{aligned}
\p(&\text{exactly 4 As, 1 B and 5 Cs}) \\
	&= \sum_{i=1}^N \p(E_i) && \text{Mutual Exclusion}\\
	&= \sum_{i=1}^N p_A ^ 4 \cdot p_B \cdot p_C^5 && \text{Sub in }\p(E_i) \\
	&= N \cdot p_A ^ 4 \cdot p_B \cdot p_C^5 && \text{Sum $N$ times}  \\
	&= {n \choose n_A, n_B, n_C} \cdot p_A ^ 4 \cdot p_B \cdot p_C^5 && \text{Perm of indistinct objects}\\
    &= {10 \choose 4, 1, 5} \cdot 0.6 ^ 4 \cdot 0.1 \cdot 0.3^5 && \text{Substitution}\\  
\end{aligned}
